abstract: Late-stage Parkinson’s disease (LSPD) presents with disabling motor and non-motor symptoms, the latter becoming dominant in the late stage. There is limited information on LSPD. This study aimed to identify common symptoms and common drug treatments of LSPD. We conducted an online survey of physicians treating patients with Parkinson’s disease in specialized palliative care across Austria, Germany and Switzerland, followed by a two-round Delphi survey involving movement disorder specialists. Consensus was defined as ≥ 75% agreement. 118 participants of 1252 contacted institutions completed the survey. In the Delphi process, eight experts out of 19 participated. Most frequently reported symptoms were dysphagia (94%), rigidity (78%), speech disorder (70%), bradykinesia (61%), dementia (74%) and constipation (64%). Most frequently used medications for motor symptom control at admission to palliative care were levodopa (96%) and rotigotine (48%). Similarly, levodopa (64%) and rotigotine (49%) were most frequently reported to be prescribed until the end of palliative care. Delphi experts agreed on the importance of oral and intestinal levodopa as well as rotigotine for the palliative care phase. Levodopa therapy should be maintained until end of life. Regarding non-motor symptom control, Delphi panelists concluded that laxatives, antipsychotics and medications for hypersalivation should be administered until end of life. Macrogol (70%) and sodium picosulfate (71%) were the most favored laxatives. Among antipsychotics quetiapine was most recommended for psychosis (76%) and delirium (59%) management. However, Delphi panelists agreed on clozapine for psychosis management and quetiapine for delirium management. For hypersalivation, consensus was reached on botulinum toxin injection. harmacological treatment of LSPD should be based on a symptom-oriented and stage-based approach. Therapy encompasses levodopa and non-dopaminergic treatments for non-motor symptom control.

title: Biosurfactants from marine thermophilic bacilli for mitigating soil dehydration and preventing plant diseases
author: Zammuto, V.
journal: International Journal of Environmental Science and Technology
abstract: To explore novel wetting and humectant agents, the hydration performances of biosurfactants (BSs) from three thermophilic bacilli, Bacillus licheniformis B3-15, B. horneckiae SBP3, and B. licheniformis s7s-1, of shallow hydrothermal vents of the Aeolian Islands (Italy) origin were investigated. Specifically, the following characteristics were evaluated in commercial soil: (i) wetting properties, measuring the reduction in water contact angle (θ) and the water-drop penetration time; (ii) moisture uptake capacity; (iii) water retention rate under high solar irradiance, and (iv) molecular-level structural dynamics hydration (water content from 0 to 160% w/w). Although all BSs were attributed to surfactin-like lipopeptides, each differed in chemical structure and consequently, in hydrating performances, with BS s7s-1 being the best wetting agent and BS SBP3 the best humectant. The molecular structural dynamics of BS s7s-1 and BS SBP3 confirmed their greater ability to capture liquid water than BS B3-15 and elucidated the molecular interaction mechanisms. Under high solar irradiance, BS s7s-1 and BS SBP3 retained water in soil (51.1 and 43.2%, respectively) more efficiently than BS B3-15 (33.5%). As assessed by the inhibition of bacterial bioluminescence and Steinernema feltiae viability, BS SBP3 and BS s7s-1 were fourfold less toxic than the lichenysin-like BS B3-15. Moreover, BS s7s-1 (500 µg mL^−1) efficiently reduced biofilm formation by two phytopathogens, Pseudomonas mediterranea (33.7%) and P. corrugata (49.4%), without affecting Bacillus subtilis . As low-toxic, wetting and humectant agents, BS s7s-1 and BS SBP3 could represent potential alternatives to industrial additives for mitigating soil dehydration and preventing plant diseases.

title: Harnessing cellulose-binding modules for advanced biosensing: principles, progress, and perspectives
author: Lee, Ae Sol
abstract: Cellulose, the most abundant natural polymer, has emerged as a sustainable platform for biosensing owing to its renewability, low cost, and biocompatibility. However, conventional probe immobilization methods on cellulose are limited by uncontrolled orientation, instability, and poor reproducibility. To overcome these barriers, cellulose-binding modules (CBMs), non-catalytic domains of carbohydrate-active enzymes, have been engineered as versatile molecular anchors. Recent studies have demonstrated that CBM fusions with enzymes, antibodies, nanobodies, nucleic acids, and reporter proteins enable oriented, high-density, and stable immobilization on cellulose scaffolds, thereby transforming cellulose from a passive carrier into an active, programmable substrate. CBM-based biosensors have been successfully applied in colorimetric, fluorescent, electrochemical, and phage-assisted platforms, achieving detection ranges from femtomolar protein biomarkers to single-colony bacterial pathogens, as well as clinically relevant monitoring of metabolites such as glucose, uric acid, and lactate. These advances underscore the potential of CBM fusion technology to improve sensitivity, reproducibility, and robustness compared to conventional cellulose-based assays. Despite these promising developments, challenges remain in clinical validation, environmental stability, and integration into portable diagnostic devices. Addressing these issues through protein engineering, nanostructured cellulose materials, and device-level innovation is expected to accelerate the translation of CBM-enabled biosensors into practical applications for healthcare, environmental monitoring, and food safety. Graphical Abstract CBM-based functional materials for enhanced sensitivity, reproducibility, and robustness of biosensing applications

title: Assessment of lavender oil, lavender nano-emulsion and its nanocomposite with chitosan as a novel bio pesticide against peach fruit fly
author: Daif, Mai K. K. A.
journal: The Journal of Basic and Applied Zoology
abstract: Over the past ten years, the peach fruit fly, Bactrocera zonata (Saunders) (Diptera: Tephritidae), has become a major pest in Egypt, causing harm to a variety of fruit crops. Traditional chemical pesticides are the main tools used in the area to control B. zonata . However, there aren’t many plant-based pesticides that are both efficient and safe for the environment that can be used to control B. zonata . The goal of this study is to create lavender nano-emulsions and lavender-chitosan nanocomposite for the first time as bio-agents against B. zonata , the peach fruit fly, in a lab setting. Lavender at a concentration of 100% demonstrated the lowest hatchability rate (58.33%) and complete larval mortality (100%). In lavender-chitosan nanocomposite and lavender nano-emulsion, 2% LEO showed no statistically significant difference was found ( p  > 0.05) low pupation rates of 14.29 and 25.98, in contrast to 88.46% for the untreated groups. The two compounds resulted in slightly lower normal emerged adults (16.70 and 24.98%), whereas the opposite was observed with the abnormal emerged adults (83.30 and 59.99%) in comparison to the untreated control (100 and 0.00%, respectively). Our findings suggest that LEO with low concentration in the form of nanoemulsion, along with chitosan composite, affects B. Zonata . Further research is underway to explore varying lavender concentrations to enhance its effectiveness against B. Zonata .

title: Green electrochemical determination of capsaicin using a sensor constructed from cattle manure and spent battery graphite
author: Wei, Ming
abstract: The recycling of agricultural and electronic waste is pivotal to realizing the circular economy and green chemistry principles. This work successfully fabricated an electrochemical sensor using cattle manure and graphite rods from spent batteries, achieving quantitative determination of capsaicin (CAP) in pickled vegetables. Distinct from previous biochar-based sensors that focus on single waste streams or multi-step modifications, this work introduces a dual-waste synergistic upcycling strategy. The CoPc@SiO_2@BC was prepared via a straightforward one-step pyrolysis process, which involved using cattle manure as the carbon source, and characterized by a suite of techniques. The CoPc@SiO_2@BC was loaded onto a graphite rod recovered from spent batteries after simple surface treatment, forming a sensor that exhibited remarkable detection performance for CAP. It demonstrated a wide linear range from 0.5 to 1500 μM, a low detection limit of 0.26 μM, along with good selectivity, repeatability, and stability, confirming its capability for real-sample analysis. This synergistic utilization of dual waste resources not only reduces electrode fabrication costs but also enhances analytical sensing performance, thereby providing a novel pathway for developing green electrochemical sensing technologies.

title: Design and characterization of a postbiotic-enriched basil seed mucilage edible coating for beef preservation: Gaussian process-based prediction
author: Ghasemi, Parisa
journal: Journal of Food Measurement and Characterization
abstract: Red meat is highly susceptible to rapid microbial growth and oxidative spoilage due to its nutrient-rich composition. Therefore, this study applied a bioactive edible coating based on Ocimum basilicum seed mucilage (OBSM) enriched with cell-free supernatant (CFS) from Lacticaseibacillus casei ANNC 26 at 0.75% and 1.5% to reduce beef spoilage during 10 days of refrigerated storage at 4 $${}^\circ C$$ . Microbiological, oxidative, physicochemical, textural, color, sensory, and Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) analyses were performed. The results showed that CFS-enriched coatings, particularly at 1.5%, significantly limited the growth of spoilage microorganisms, with the lowest total viable count recorded in the OBSM + 1.5% CFS treatment at the end of storage (6.11 ± 0.32 log colony forming unit (CFU)/g) compared with the control (9.48 ± 0.45 log CFU/g). The antioxidant activity of CFS bioactives improved beef oxidative stability by reducing the increase in peroxide value (PV) and thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS), which reached 5.36 ± 0.24 meq O₂/kg fat and 1.03 ± 0.05 mg MDA/kg in the OBSM + 1.5% CFS treatment, respectively, compared with 8.82 ± 0.35 meq O₂/kg fat and 1.74 ± 0.12 mg MDA/kg in the control. Furthermore, the findings indicated that the treated samples exhibited superior performance in maintaining pH, moisture content, texture, color attributes, and overall sensory acceptability. GPR was applied to predict twelve food quality parameters. The models demonstrated exceptional accuracy for physicochemical attributes (pH: mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) 0.17%, hardness: 0.08%, moisture: 0.01%) and reliable performance for microbiological indicators (total viable count (TVC): 3.93%, fungi: 2.83%). Overall acceptance was predicted with 4.76% MAPE and 0.96 R², confirming GPR as a robust predictive tool for quality assessment. Overall, OBSM coating enriched with 1.5% CFS can be considered an effective natural strategy for improving the refrigerated shelf life and quality preservation of beef. Graphical Abstract

title: Poly(hydroxybutyrate-co-hydroxyvalerate) Composite Membrane Containing Tetracycline Microspheres and Andrographolide for the Treatment of Periodontitis
author: Panith, Nootchanartch
journal: Journal of Polymers and the Environment
abstract: Guided tissue regeneration (GTR) membrane plays an important role in barrier function and regeneration of supporting cells for periodontitis treatment. However, bacterial infection is currently considered as the major reason for GTR failure in clinical applications. Our work is focused on formulating a composite GTR membrane composed of a biodegradable polymer poly(hydroxybutyrate-co-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV), co-loaded with the antibiotic tetracycline encapsulated in microspheres (TCMS) and the bioactive molecule andrographolide (AG), denoted as PHBV:TCMS/AG membrane. The encapsulation efficiency of TC and AG in PHBV:TCMS/AG membrane was found to be 86.4% and 81.1%, respectively. The membrane morphology, surface hydrophilicity and mechanical properties were investigated. The PHBV:TCMS/AG membrane showed controlled release of TC and AG over 18 days, and exhibited antibacterial activities against periodontitis-causing bacteria Porphyromonas gingivalis and Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans . Thus, the composite PHBV:TCMS/AG membrane demonstrates sustained dual-drug release and its efficacy in suppressing the growth of periodontal pathogens.

title: Can batteries be fully sustainable?
author: Ojodun, Oluwasegun Emmanuel
abstract: Concerns over the environmental impact, supply chain vulnerability, and long-term availability of conventional lithium-ion battery (LIB) materials have intensified interest in sustainable alternatives. This review defines a fully sustainable battery as one in which all components are derived from renewable materials and produced through eco-friendly processes across their entire lifecycle, consistent with the ISO 14044:2006 LCA framework. The current state of partially sustainable batteries is evaluated against this definition through a critical review of recent advances in biomass-derived carbon anodes, organic cathode materials, biopolymer gel electrolytes, cellulose-based separators, bio-derived binders, and carbonaceous current collectors across lithium-ion, sodium-ion (SIB), and aqueous zinc-ion (ZIB) battery chemistries. Key findings include the cost and carbon footprint competitiveness of biomass-derived hard carbon anodes with synthetic graphite ($1.72 kg^−1 vs $4.97 kg^−1; 3.2 vs 25.1 kg CO₂-eq kg^−1), the ionic conductivity competitiveness of biopolymer gel electrolytes with conventional liquid electrolytes (up to 11 mS cm^−1), and the consistent superiority of cellulose-based separators over commercial polypropylene in thermal stability, electrolyte wettability, and biodegradability. This review makes an original contribution by identifying four challenges that prevent the integration of these components into a fully sustainable battery. The costs, sustainability, and lifecycle assessments of LIBs, SIBs, and ZIBs are comparatively evaluated using available LCA data, and prospects for sustainable battery recycling are assessed. Based on this analysis, five research directions are proposed, with SIBs and aqueous ZIBs identified as the most viable configurations for fully sustainable batteries given their compatibility with bio-derived materials and lower lifecycle environmental impact.

title: Low-intensity pasture management sustain dung beetle taxonomic and functional diversity in Cerrado/Caatinga transition zones
author: Maciel, Rafaella
abstract: Abstract Increasing grazing pressure for food production is a major challenge for biodiversity conservation in tropical dryland, particularly in ecologically complex transition zones that harbor substantial global biodiversity. Despite their high conservation value, the effects of grazing management on biodiversity in drylands remain poorly understood. We investigated how land-use intensity and local environmental metrics influence both taxonomic and functional diversity of dung beetles in native habitats and pastures under contrasting management intensities within a Cerrado–Caatinga transition zone in Brazil. Species richness was significantly higher in native areas and low-intensity pastures than in high-intensity pastures. Vegetation heterogeneity negatively affected the abundance of small- and medium-sized dung beetles in native areas and high-intensity pastures, while exerting positive effects in low-intensity pastures. Soil sand content showed contrasting effects on functional richness, increasing it in low-intensity pastures but reducing it in high-intensity pastures. Although dung beetle species composition differed among land-use types, low-intensity pastures shared a substantially greater number of species with native habitats than high-intensity pastures. Implications for insect conservation Our results demonstrate that low-intensity pasture management sustains both taxonomic and functional diversity of dung beetles and enhances habitat permeability for species originating from native environments. Promoting less intensive grazing practices in dryland transition regions can therefore represent an effective strategy to reconcile livestock production with insect conservation and the maintenance of key ecosystem services.

title: Nanocellulose stabilized liquid metal Pickering emulsions
author: Wang, Qianqian
abstract: Gallium-based liquid metals possess high electrical conductivity and fluidity, but their enormous surface tension makes it difficult to disperse them uniformly in aqueous media. In this work, five types of nanocellulose, namely, cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs), cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs), TEMPO‑oxidized cellulose nanofibrils (TCNFs), quaternized cellulose nanofibrils (QCNFs), and bacterial cellulose (BC), were compared as interfacial stabilizers for gallium liquid metal (LM) Pickering emulsions. The nanocellulose/liquid metal Pickering emulsions were prepared by probe ultrasonication and characterized by optical microscopy, dynamic light scattering/zeta potential, TEM, FTIR, XPS, and TGA. All nanocellulose/liquid metal droplets formed core–shell structures, suppressing droplet coalescence. The stability of nanocellulose stabilized liquid metal Pickering emulsions followed the order BC > TCNFs > CNFs > QCNFs > CNCs. XPS analyses revealed that functional groups on nanocellulose interact with the gallium oxide skin via electrostatic attraction and coordination, and TGA indicated that the composites maintain good thermal stability and form gallium oxide at high temperatures. These results demonstrate that renewable nanocellulose can serve as green and effective stabilizers for high‑surface‑energy liquid metal, enabling long‑term stable Pickering emulsions. Graphical abstract

title: Adaptation mechanisms of ANAMMOX bacteria to extreme environments
author: Pathania, Ruchi
abstract: Anaerobic ammonium oxidation (ANAMMOX) bacteria (AnAOB) play a vital role in the global nitrogen cycle and have emerged as a promising alternative for sustainable nitrogen removal in wastewater treatment. They directly convert ammonium and nitrite into dinitrogen gas under anaerobic conditions, without the need for high energy and external carbon associated with conventional nitrification-denitrification. With increasing global demands to mitigate nutrient pollution and improve water quality, a deeper understanding of AnAOB has become both scientifically significant and practically necessary. Despite the successful application of anammox technology across a diverse wastewater treatment streams, the mechanisms underlying their translation into predictive, scalable process control remain poorly understood. So, it’s imperative to develop an understanding of their enzymatic systems, metabolic pathways, cellular structure, and adaptive responses, which provides deeper insights into optimizing ANAMMOX-based biotechnologies for wastewater treatment for commercial viability. Therefore, this review reports strategies to reframe AnAOB resilience developed by analysing physiological, molecular, and ecological adaptation mechanisms that enable AnAOB to survive and function under extreme environmental conditions. A conceptual framework has been developed using three key strategies: (i) membrane remodeling through changes in membrane fluidity, transporter activity, and ladderane lipid composition; secondly, (ii) metabolic flux redistribution involving regulation of stress response proteins, metabolic flexibility, and energy conservation; and (iii) biofilm formation and interactions within microbial consortia which is providing insights regarding quorum sensing and community cross feeding. Furthermore, detailed insights into their substrate preferences, growth rates, stress responses, and microbial interactions can advance reactor designs, operational stability, and industrial scalability. Final, this review highlights the major knowledge gaps and challenges that limit its broader implementation and discusses future research directions required to advance predictive process control and next-generation ANAMMOX-based wastewater treatment systems. Graphical abstract

title: Nanoparticle-reinforced polysaccharide–protein composite hydrogels: synthesis, structural integrity, and sustained release behavior
author: Azaza, Youssra Ben
abstract: Designing bio-nanocomposite hydrogels that combine structural performance with controlled bioactive release remains a key challenge in functional polymer science. In this work, we developed a crosslinked nanocomposite hydrogel system based on chitosan-tuna protein interactions, in which chitosan nanoparticles (CsNP) and phycocyanin-loaded chitosan nanoparticles (Ph-CsNP) were incorporated as reinforcing nanoparticle agents. The nanoparticles were first prepared by ionotropic gelation and thoroughly characterized in terms of colloidal properties such as particle size, zeta potential, and polydispersity index, as well as encapsulation efficiency. The resulting Ph-CsNP were then incorporated into the matrix of a glutaraldehyde crosslinked composite, and the effect of nanoparticle loading on the viscoelastic, mechanical, structural and thermal properties of the hydrogel network was systematically explored. The results revealed that both CsNP and Ph-CsNP are reinforcing agents, enhancing the network integrity and swelling capacity, and thus emphasizing the interactions between the polysaccharide and the protein at the interface, which define the composite architecture. Release kinetics analysis revealed that phycocyanin release from both formulations followed a diffusion-controlled Fickian mechanism, whereas incorporation into the hydrogel matrix further prolonged release and improved bioactive retention in the HG-20(Ph-CsNP) formulation. Overall, these findings highlight the potential of incorporating nanoparticle reinforcement with biopolymer composite engineering to develop tunable polymeric matrices exhibiting programmable release behavior. Such systems represent promising candidates for functional biomaterials and controlled bioactive delivery, although additional biological studies are needed to validate their biomedical potential.

title: Improvement in Chloride-Induced Mild Steel Corrosion Mitigation Using a Surfactant Intercalated Montmorillonite
author: Yemene, Astrée Lottie Djuffo
abstract: The corrosion inhibitory properties of a hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide intercalated montmorillonite (HDTMAB@Mt) against XC38 steel corrosion were investigated. Montmorillonite and HDTMAB@Mt were characterised for crystallinity, morphology, functional group and thermal stability. The electrochemical properties of these materials were equally investigated, providing insight into adsorption, diffusion and interfacial charge transfer phenomena. Then, the HDTMAB@Mt composite was used as a corrosion mitigator for XC38 steel corrosion. A maximum inhibition efficiency of 96.65% was obtained. Polarisation curve analyses revealed that the inhibitor acts through a mixed-type mechanism, affecting both anodic and cathodic reactions. The inhibitor’s adsorption behaviour was best described by the Langmuir isotherm. Temperature-dependent studies allowed the determination of an activation energy of 71.96 kJ/mol, an enthalpy of adsorption of 69.32 kJ/mol, an entropy of adsorption of − 23.01 J/mol/K and an adsorption free energy of − 12.40 kJ/mol, indicating a predominantly physisorption mechanism. From this study, the HDTMAB@Mt material stands out as a highly efficient and low-cost XC38 steel corrosion mitigator in acidic environments. Graphical Abstract

title: Balancing ion selectivity and flux through crystallinity engineering in cellulose nanofluidic membranes for osmotic energy harvesting
author: Wang, Jian
abstract: Cellulose-based nanofluidic membranes are promising for osmotic energy harvesting, but high crystallinity often suppresses ion transport and reduces energy-conversion efficiency. Here, we investigate how crosslinking-regulated cellulose crystallinity affects ion-transport behavior by constructing membranes with tunable chemical crosslinking density. The results show that crosslinking-dependent crystallinity strongly influences the selectivity-flux trade-off and, in turn, the power output. At the optimized crystallinity achieved through crosslinking regulation, the cellulose membrane exhibits the best overall ion-management performance, delivering 3.69 W m^−2 in a 50-fold salinity gradient system, approximately 265% higher than that of the highly crystalline membrane. 13 series-connected single-membrane units provide stable outputs of 3.2 μA and 1.5 V for over 2500 s, supporting preliminary demonstrations of small-device operation and capacitor-assisted energy storage. This work provides a crystallinity-engineering route for cellulose-based membranes toward efficient and sustainable osmotic energy conversion. Graphical abstract

title: Soil Remediation Technologies for Contaminant and Pathogen Control in Southern Africa
author: Mugwagwa, Lindleen R.
abstract: This chapter reviews soil remediation techniques tailored to address contamination and pathogen risks in the Southern Africa context. It examines the primary sources of soil pollution such as mining, industrial activities, agricultural inputs and improper waste disposal and evaluates their impacts on environmental quality, agricultural productivity and public health, with emphasis on region-specific challenges. The potential of key remediation approaches, such as physical methods (e.g. excavation and containment), thermal treatment, chemical treatment (e.g. stabilisation and immobilisation) and bioremediation in decontaminating the polluted soil (heavy metals, pesticides, hydrocarbons and pathogens), is discussed. Emerging applications of nanotechnology in contaminant removal are explored for their potential to enhance remediation efficiency. Integrated strategies combining these methods are discussed to optimise outcomes in diverse Southern African ecosystems. The chapter highlights monitoring and assessment to evaluate remediation success, addressing region-specific issues like resource constraints and scalability. The chapter concludes by outlining future directions focused on sustainable, locally adapted technologies that align with regional environmental conditions and development priorities. It provides practical, evidence-based insights to support environmental scientists, practitioners and policymakers engaged in soil contamination management and pathogen control in Southern Africa.

title: GO-Modified Pectin-Based Biopolymer Hydrogel for Sustainable Basic Fuchsin Removal from Wastewater: Process Optimization and Multiscale Mechanistic Insights
author: Aljeboree, Aseel M.
journal: Journal of Polymers and the Environment
abstract: A novel graphene oxide-functionalized pectin-graft-poly(acrylic acid-co-polyvinyl alcohol) hydrogel composite (PEC-g-(AAc/PVA)/GO) was successfully fabricated via free-radical polymerization and evaluated as an efficient adsorbent for the removal of Basic Fuchsin (BF) from aqueous media. Comprehensive physicochemical characterization using FTIR, XRD, TGA, FESEM-EDX, BET, and TEM confirmed the successful formation of a porous, heterogeneous, and thermally stable hydrogel network enriched with abundant adsorption-active functional groups. Swelling studies demonstrated enhanced hydrophilicity and network flexibility, with maximum swelling observed under neutral conditions. Process optimisation using response surface methodology based on the Box–Behnken design identified optimum adsorption conditions at pH 7, 30 °C, 60 min contact time, 0.08 g adsorbent dosage, and 900 mg L⁻^1 initial dye concentration. Adsorption kinetics were best described by the pseudo-first-order model (R^2 = 0.9768–0.9987), while equilibrium data were most accurately represented by the Freundlich isotherm model (R^2 = 0.9896–0.9997), indicating multilayer adsorption on a heterogeneous surface. The maximum adsorption capacity predicted by the Langmuir model was 1198.11 mg.g⁻^1. Thermodynamic parameters (ΔH = + 10.67 kJ mol⁻^1, ΔS = + 93.53 J K⁻^1 mol⁻^1, and ΔG = − 31.23 to − 36.87 kJ mol⁻^1) confirmed a spontaneous and endothermic adsorption process. The developed hydrogel retained more than 85% of its adsorption efficiency after ten regeneration cycles and exhibited excellent performance in real water samples. Molecular dynamics simulations and DFT calculations (ωB97XD/6-31G(d,p)) revealed stable dye–surface interactions, governed predominantly by dispersion forces, complemented by electrostatic interactions and hydrogen bonding, with significant electron-density redistribution upon complex formation. Preliminary economic assessment further demonstrated the practical feasibility of the developed material. These findings establish PEC-g-(AAc/PVA)/GO as a highly efficient, reusable, and scalable adsorbent for advanced wastewater treatment applications.

title: Corrosion Inhibition of Q275 Carbon Steel in Hydrochloric Acid Using Poly(Acrylic Acid): Experimental, Surface, and Statistical Optimization Study
author: Udunwa, Daniel Iheanacho
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance
abstract: Polymeric inhibitors have emerged as effective and environmentally sustainable alternatives for mitigating metal corrosion. In this study, poly(acrylic acid) (PAA) was evaluated as a green corrosion inhibitor for Q275 carbon steel in 2.0 M hydrochloric acid solution. The inhibition performance of PAA was systematically investigated using gravimetric analysis (GT), steady-state potential (SSP) measurements, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and potentiodynamic polarization (PDP) techniques. The results demonstrated that PAA significantly reduced the corrosion rate, acting as a mixed-type inhibitor by suppressing both anodic and cathodic reactions, with a maximum inhibition efficiency of 96.41%. Response surface methodology was employed to correlate experimental and computational parameters, yielding a predicted efficiency of 96.62%, which was in close agreement with the experimental value of 96.47 ± 0.08%, with a minimal deviation of 0.16%, thereby confirming the model’s reliability. The adsorption behavior followed the Langmuir isotherm, indicating the formation of a uniform monolayer on the steel surface. Surface characterization using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), and x-ray diffraction (XRD) confirmed the formation of a protective film, consistent with the electrochemical results. Additionally, quantum chemical analysis identified the active adsorption sites within the PAA molecule, supporting a synergistic inhibition mechanism involving both chemisorption and physisorption. Graphical Abstract

title: Structural Reinforcement of Alginate Biopolymer Matrices with Silk Fibroin for Stable Whole-Cell Biocatalysts
author: Imanparast, Somaye
journal: Journal of Polymers and the Environment
abstract: Whole-cell immobilization provides an attractive alternative to purified enzyme systems, although matrix instability and mass-transfer limitations often restrict industrial application. In this study, silk fibroin was integrated into calcium alginate microbeads to fabricate a mechanically reinforced composite for immobilization of heat-treated glucose isomerase (GI; EC 5.3.1.5)-producing Streptomyces olivochromogenes . FTIR analysis suggested additional intermolecular interactions between fibroin and alginate, consistent with improved structural cohesion of the composite matrix. Compared with alginate-only beads, fibroin-containing composites exhibited enhanced compressive resistance, improved pore interconnectivity, and superior structural integrity during repeated batch operation. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) demonstrated increased thermal stability of fibroin-containing matrices, while silica incorporation further increased residual mass (38.08%) and delayed thermal degradation. However, the denser silica-containing matrix was associated with higher apparent K m values and lower catalytic activity, suggesting increased diffusion resistance. Under reaction conditions of 60 °C, 3 M glucose, and pH 7.0, fibroin–alginate immobilized cells retained more than 80% of their initial activity after 20 reuse cycles and maintained approximately 91% activity after four months of storage at 25 °C. These results demonstrate that fibroin reinforcement enhances the structural stability of whole-cell immobilization matrices while preserving effective substrate accessibility, providing a reusable biopolymer platform for industrial glucose isomerization.

title: Sustained-Release Polymeric Submicron Microspheres of Valsartan: Formulation, Characterization, and Release Kinetics
author: Mahmood, Syed
abstract: Valsartan (VAL), an angiotensin II receptor blocker widely used in the management of hypertension and heart failure, exhibits poor oral bioavailability due to its low aqueous solubility, extensive first-pass metabolism, and short elimination half-life. The present study aimed to optimize a multi-polymeric carrier system comprising chitosan, sodium alginate, and polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP K30) to fabricate sub-micron microspheres with high entrapment and sustained release. Microspheres were prepared using the oil-in-water solvent emulsion evaporation technique employing chitosan, sodium alginate, and polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP K30) as the polymeric matrix. The prepared formulations were evaluated for particle size, polydispersity index (PDI), zeta potential, and entrapment efficiency, followed by physicochemical characterization using Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC), X-ray Powder Diffraction (XRD), and Environmental Scanning Electron Microscopy (ESEM). The optimized formulation (A3) exhibited a mean particle size of 499.5 ± 29.5 nm, PDI of 0.370 ± 0.029, zeta potential of + 51.33 ± 1.25 mV, and a high entrapment efficiency of 94.98 ± 0.44%. FTIR analysis confirmed intermolecular interactions between valsartan and the polymer matrix, while DSC and XRD analyses demonstrated reduced crystallinity and successful molecular dispersion of valsartan within the polymers. ESEM images revealed spherical, smooth-surfaced microspheres with minimal aggregation. Stability studies conducted over 60 days at 4 °C demonstrated acceptable physical stability without significant changes in particle size ( p  > 0.05). In vitro drug release studies showed sustained and pH-responsive release behaviour, with the highest cumulative drug release observed at pH 6.8 (95.84% at 24 h), indicating enhanced release under intestinal conditions. Release kinetic modelling demonstrated diffusion-controlled release at acidic pH and anomalous transport at intestinal pH. Overall, the developed multi-polymeric sub-micron microsphere system represents a promising strategy for improving valsartan solubility, stability, and sustained oral delivery, with potential to enhance therapeutic efficacy and patient compliance.

title: AI-enabled discovery and biochemical optimization of minibinders targeting cancer cell-surface proteins
author: Broske, Bianca
abstract: Experimental validation and functional optimization remain bottlenecks in AI-based protein design. We present a scalable workflow for developing AI-designed minibinders against cancer-associated surface proteins. Screening thousands of designs using mammalian cell-surface display identifies several high-affinity PD-L1 minibinders but far fewer for CD276 (B7-H3) and VTCN1 (B7-H4), highlighting substantial target dependence. Interface predicted template modeling (ipTM) scores generated by Chai-1 with ESM embeddings correlate with binding success and capture deleterious effects of interface mutations. Fluorophore-labeled AI-minibinders enable flow-cytometric staining comparable to conventional antibodies. However, when incorporated into chimeric antigen receptors (CAR), some show poor cell-surface trafficking and limited functionality. Redesign through a genetic algorithm-based diversification strategy that preserves the binding interface while changing non-binding surfaces experimentally reveals an isoelectric point (pI) window that improves CAR expression and enhances target-selective tumor cell killing. Our findings identify biochemical optimization beyond the binding interface as a critical requirement for translating AI-minibinders into functional applications. In this work the authors present a scalable mammalian cell-display workflow to identify AI-designed minibinders against cancer surface targets. AI-guided optimization beyond the binding interface improves their expression as chimeric antigen receptors and target-selective killing.

title: Nanotechnology and Biosensor: Current Gold Nanoparticles Modification in EIS-Based Immunosensor for Infectious Disease Detection
author: Juraimi, Nur Uzma Ishami
abstract: The emergence and re-emergence of infectious diseases have caused great concern for global organizations due to their destructive impacts on health, the economy, and human survivability, following the fast-evolving and adaptive characteristics of pathogens. This concern highlights the urgent need for the development of point-of-care diagnostic tools for rapid and reliable screening of pathogens, which can be applied widely without geographic barriers. An electrochemical impedance spectroscopy-based immunosensor is considered an effective alternative to conventional methods for decentralized diagnostics, owing to its cost efficiency, simplicity, sensitivity, and label-free potential. Incorporating nanotechnology into an impedimetric immunosensor can enhance reliability, but it requires careful consideration of electrode fabrication and surface modification. Thus, this review provides insights into the integration of notable nanomaterials, gold nanoparticles, highlighting their important characteristics such as high surface areas, conductivity, and biocompatibility in enhancing the overall performance of the EIS-based immunosensor. This review further discussed the recent application of this integrated system in diagnosing infectious diseases, including viral, bacterial, and parasitic infections. Despite different AuNP modification strategies, studies reported levels of detection ranging from 5.77 × 10⁻^7 to 3.54 × 10^3 ng mL⁻^1 and 15 CFU mL⁻^1, high sensitivity, and short detection times (15 min to 60 min), crucial for POC tool development. This review also discussed the current limitations and future directions for establishing a robust, clinically validated diagnostic platform. Overall, the potential of integrating nanotechnology into immunosensors is emphasized to advance biotechnology and translate it into healthcare settings. Graphical abstract Summary of the integration of AuNP-modified electrode surface into EIS-based immunosensor and its current application in detecting different infectious diseases in humans carried by viruses, bacteria, and parasites. The performance of nano-modified immunosensors was evaluated, which is crucial for advancing the development of a POC diagnostic platform, in accordance with the ‘ASSURED’ criteria introduced by the WHO.

title: The evaluation of biological effects of artesunate on ovarian cancer using three-dimensional cell culture methods
author: Yuan, Yijun
abstract: Ovarian cancer (OC) is one of the most aggressive malignancies, with high mortality rates largely attributed to late-stage diagnosis, tumor heterogeneity, recurrence, and resistance to chemotherapy. Artesunate (ART), a water-soluble derivative traditionally used to treat malaria, has recently gained attention as a promising anticancer agent. Recently, studies have shown that ART can inhibit the migration and invasion of cancer cells. However, theses studies are always based on conventional two-dimensional (2D) culture models, which neglect the complex interactions between cells and the extracellular matrix (ECM) or in vivo microenvironment. To address these challenges, in this study, honeycomb-like gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) hydrogel microspheres as a three-dimensional (3D) culture platform were introduced to mimic the native ECM microenvironment and assess the effects of ART on ovarian cancer cells. The results showed that these GelMA microspheres exhibited a uniform and highly porous structure, which supported cell adhesion, proliferation, and migration. Notably, 3D culture promoted DNA synthesis and induced G1-to-S phase transition, indicating enhanced proliferative capacity. Furthermore, ovarian cancer cells cultured in 3D exhibited stronger invasive and chemoresistant phenotypes. RNA sequencing revealed that after ART treatment, tumor-related proliferation and invasion genes of ovarian cancer cells were significantly up-regulated under 3D culture compared with 2D culture. This might be related to the up-regulation of TNF signaling pathway, NF-kappa B signaling pathway, and Pl3K-Akt signaling pathway. Correspondly, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) of ovarian cancer cells was markedly enhanced when cultured on GelMA hydrogel microspheres after ART treatment. These effects might be attributed to the altered microenvironment provided by the GelMA hydrogel microspheres, which could be responsible for the enhanced resistance of ovarian cancer cells to ART. These findings suggest that, compared to traditional 2D. These findings suggest that, compared to traditional 2D culture, the 3D extracellular matrix-based system better mimics the in vivo tumor architecture, thereby improving the sensitivity of anticancer drug screening and offering a more reliable platform for evaluating drug resistance and tumor cell heterogeneity.

title: Strategies for Innovations in Algal Biomass Utilisation: From Biofuel Production to Environmental Sustainability
author: Hussain, Mudasir
abstract: Algal biomass is a versatile feedstock for renewable fuels and bioproducts, but its technical potential does not automatically translate into environmental or commercial viability. This review critically integrates the complete algal-biofuel chain, including strain selection, cultivation-system design, harvesting and dewatering, genetic and metabolic engineering, biomass pretreatment, biochemical conversion, and thermochemical conversion. Unlike reviews that examine individual unit operations or single fuel routes, the present work compares technologies using common decision criteria: biomass and product productivity, moisture tolerance, energy and chemical demand, scalability, technological maturity, environmental burden, and economic feasibility. Open ponds, closed photobioreactors, and hybrid cultivation strategies are evaluated in relation to contamination control, productivity, capital intensity, and operational energy. Pretreatment methods are assessed according to cell-disruption efficiency, net energy recovery, reagent requirements, downstream compatibility, and industrial applicability. Conversion pathways are then compared to show that no single route is optimal for all feedstocks: transesterification is most defensible for consistently lipid-rich biomass, anaerobic digestion is suitable for wet residues and wastewater-grown biomass, and hydrothermal liquefaction is promising for wet whole-biomass conversion but requires effective biocrude upgrading and nutrient recovery. The review further examines life-cycle trade-offs, water and nutrient demand, carbon accounting, production costs, policy dependence, and the role of co-products. A structured research roadmap is proposed to move the field from isolated yield maximisation toward integrated, seasonally validated, mass- and energy-balanced algal biorefineries. Graphical Abstract

title: Cryoprotective effects of soluble soybean polysaccharides on bighead carp surimi: Impacts of molecular weight variations
author: Gao, Wenhong
journal: Journal of Food Measurement and Characterization
abstract: Molecular-weight-dependent cryoprotection of SSPS for surimi was clarified. Low-MW SSPS preserved myosin integrity during frozen storage. Multiscale mechanism: H-bonding, water regulation, interfacial effects. A Diffusion-Penetration-Anchoring model was established for SSPS cryoprotection. Soluble soybean polysaccharides (SSPS, 5025.24 kDa) with different molecular weights were investigated for their cryoprotective effects on surimi. SSPS-U (4384.77 kDa) and SSPS-H (3218.14 kDa) were prepared via ultrasound and ultrasound-assisted hydrogen peroxide degradation, respectively. A 3% polysaccharide was added to SSPS surimi, SSPS-U surimi, and SSPS-H surimi, respectively; and stored at -18 °C for 12 weeks. Their cryoprotective effects on myofibrillar proteins (MPs) were systematically evaluated. Results showed that SSPS-H exhibited the optimal protective performance. After 12 weeks of frozen storage, the Ca²⁺-ATPase activity retention in the SSPS-H group reached 50.66% (vs. 25.98% in the control), while the decline in total sulfhydryl content was reduced by 33.32%. SDS-PAGE confirmed the inhibition of myosin heavy chain degradation, and Raman spectroscopy indicated that SSPS-H effectively mitigated alterations in disulfide bonds, aromatic residues and secondary structure. Mechanistically, the enhanced efficacy of SSPS-H was attributed to its improved molecular flexibility and diffusivity, enabling penetration into protein matrices and formation of hydrogen-bonding networks with polar residues. Meanwhile, SSPS-H regulated water distribution by converting free water into immobilized and non-freezable states, thereby suppressing ice crystal formation and structural damage. In contrast, high-molecular-weight SSPS exhibited limited interfacial interactions due to steric hindrance.

title: Oyster mushroom (Pleurotus ostreatus) polysaccharides as a natural alternative to phosphate in chicken nugget formulations: enhancing quality and oxidative stability
author: Yüncü-Boyacı, Özlem
journal: Journal of Food Measurement and Characterization
abstract: This study investigates the potential of oyster mushroom ( Pleurotus ostreatus ) polysaccharide extract (MPE) as a phosphate replacer in chicken nuggets, focusing on its effects on physicochemical and textural properties, oxidative stability, and sensory characteristics. MPE showed significant antioxidant activity, with a total phenolic content of 56.23 mg GAE/g and high DPPH, ABTS, and FRAP values. Incorporating MPE at different levels (0.5%, 1%, 1.5%) affected chemical composition, reducing fat content and increasing dietary fiber, with MP3 having the highest fiber content. Cooking characteristics, such as yield, moisture, and fat retention, improved with higher MPE concentrations. MPE also influenced texture, reducing hardness, springiness, and chewiness, particularly at higher levels. While STPP improved fat distribution and gel network strength, 1.5% MPE resulted in an irregular structure and reduced elasticity, suggesting an impact of MPE’s protein and polysaccharide content on the gel structure. MPE addition lowered pH values and generally produced lower L* and higher b* values compared to controls. Sensory analysis indicated that MPE positively affected flavor, juiciness, and acceptability, with MP2 and MP3 formulations preferred during extended storage. DSC measurements showed that MPE raised the oxidation onset temperature, enhancing oxidative stability, confirmed by lower TBARS values in MPE samples. This study suggests that MPE can serve as an effective, natural alternative to phosphates in chicken nugget production, enhancing nutritional quality, oxidative stability, and sensory properties.

title: Chitosan-derived antibacterial and antifungal agents: a review of recent strategies for activity enhancement
author: Felemban, Mohammed Fareed
abstract: Chitosan (CS), a naturally occurring biopolymer derived from chitin, has garnered significant attention for its intrinsic antimicrobial properties, biocompatibility, and biodegradability. However, its limited solubility and relatively moderate activity under physiological conditions have prompted the development of various strategies to enhance its antimicrobial performance. This review provides an up-to-date overview (2024–2025) of recent advances in the design and modification of CS-based materials to improve their antimicrobial efficacy against a broad spectrum of pathogens. Emphasis is placed on chemical modifications, such as quaternization, carboxymethylation, and the grafting of functional groups, as well as on physical strategies, including nanoparticle formulation, hybridization with metal ions or oxides, and incorporation into composite materials. The review also discusses the mechanisms by which these modifications enhance antimicrobial action, along with their potential applications in biomedical devices, wound dressings, food packaging, and water treatment.

title: Improving the structural, physical, and thermal properties of polyacrylic acid via Pb_0.9Mg_0.1O NPs incorporation for micro-dielectric devices
author: Alshamari, Awatif
journal: Journal of Materials Science: Materials in Electronics
abstract: This study is devoted to investigating the structure, optical, and dielectric characterization of polyacrylic acid (PAA) reinforced with Mg-doped PbO nanoparticles (PbMgO NPs). The fillers and nanocomposite films were prepared by facile chemical methods. The structural characterization, morphology, chemical composition, interactions, and complexation between PAA chains and PbMgO NPs were investigated using XRD, FTIR spectroscopy, FE-SEM, and EDX techniques. These techniques revealed the amorphous character of PAA, the presence of Mg in the α -PbO/ β -PbO NPs mixed phase with homogeneous dispersion, and the interactions between NPs and the COOH group of PAA. UV–vis spectroscopy showed a decrease in transmittance from 91 to 40%, an increase in the refractive index, and a reduction of the optical band gap from 4.7 to 4.0 eV. The influence of PbMgO NPs content on the absorption index and Urbach energy of PAA was reported. The dielectric parameters: dielectric permittivity, energy dissipation, electric modulus, and AC conductivity were investigated in the 70 Hz–7.0 MHz frequency ( f ) range and from 298 to 408 K. These parameters showed strong dependence on f , temperature, and PbMgO NPs content. The maximum conductivity increased from (3.9–12) × 10⁻^4 S·m⁻^1 to (6.91–17.1) × 10⁻^4 S·m⁻^1 at 6.0 wt% PbMgO NPs content. The dielectric permittivity was enhanced with low energy dissipation. The electric modulus formalism, conduction mechanism, and relaxation phenomena, as well as the Argand plots, were analyzed. Moreover, the thermal analysis was performed in the temperature range of 30–600 °C. The findings reveal substantial improvements in the optical, dielectric parameters, and thermal properties of PbMgO/PAA, making these nanocomposites the best candidates for advanced micro/optoelectronics and energy storage systems.

title: Chitin and Chitosan in Biomedical Science: Structural Modifications, Functional Properties, Therapeutic Applications, and Future Perspectives
author: Qadir, Amjad Mahmood
abstract: Chitin and chitosan are naturally sourced, biodegradable biopolymers that have garnered heightened interest in biomedical research due to their biocompatibility, chemical adaptability, and extensive therapeutic applications. This review summarises their structural characteristics, physicochemical attributes, natural origins, and traditional as well as eco-friendly extraction techniques, highlighting the impact of deacetylation degree, molecular weight, crystallinity, and chemical alterations on solubility, bioadhesion, antimicrobial efficacy, and mechanical properties. It additionally emphasises significant biomedical uses, such as drug delivery, wound repair, haemostasis, tissue engineering, antimicrobial and antiviral treatments, and regenerative medicine, while also addressing functionalised derivatives and nanocarrier systems aimed at enhancing targeting, controlled release, and effectiveness. Notwithstanding encouraging preclinical and clinical results, many obstacles persist, such as batch inconsistency, restricted solubility, scale issues, regulatory constraints, and reproducibility concerns. In summary, chitin and chitosan are very promising sustainable biomaterials; however, additional standardisation, safety evaluations, and translational research are required to facilitate wider clinical and industrial application.

title: Edible Nanozymes as Functional Nutrients: Redefining Antioxidant and Metabolic Roles in Food Systems
author: Singh, Lovepreet
abstract: With the increasing demand for functional foods, novel nutrition strategies that extend beyond antioxidant supplementation are being explored. One such nanotechnology-enabled approach is the development of edible nanozymes, enzyme-mimicking nanomaterials capable of catalytically regulating oxidative and metabolic processes in food and living systems. In contrast to conventional antioxidants, which are depleted after scavenging reactive oxygen species, nanozymes maintain catalytic function to dynamically regulate redox balance and improve functionality. This review highlights recent developments in the past decade for food-compatible nanozymes, including metal oxide-, carbon-, hybrid-, and biogenic nanozymes, with regard to synthesis, stability, edibility, and application in various food matrices. This review focuses on the current research and development of edible nanozymes, particularly emphasizing their superoxide dismutase-, catalase-, and peroxidase-like activity and stability under gastrointestinal conditions. It explores the nanozyme–gut–metabolism axis, elucidating interactions with gut microbiota, oxidative stress modulation, nutrient bioavailability, and glucose and lipid metabolism regulation. The proposed “Catalytic Nutrition Framework” envisions edible nanozymes as active nutritional agents, encompassing the synergy of food functionality and metabolic health. This review considers the potential of edible nanozymes in disease prevention, personalized nutrition, and the enhancement of functional foods, addressing concerns of safety, digestibility, regulations, and chronic exposure. By positioning nanozymes as functional nutrients or additives, this work offers a novel perspective for catalytic and precision nutrition. Graphical Abstract

title: Sustainable stabilization of silty sand using Terrazyme: effects on mechanical and hydraulic properties
author: Singh, Vikash
abstract: This study evaluates the effectiveness of Terrazyme, a plant-derived bioenzymatic soil stabilizer, in improving the geotechnical performance of silty sand collected from the Lucknow region, India. The selected soil, characterized by intermediate gradation and low bearing capacity, exhibits relatively low strength, high compressibility, high permeability, and susceptibility to deformation under applied loading, thereby posing challenges for infrastructure development. To address these limitations, varying dosages of Terrazyme were incorporated, and their effects on key engineering properties, including Atterberg limits, permeability, Unconfined Compressive Strength (UCS), and durability, were systematically investigated. The experimental results demonstrated significant improvements in strength and durability, accompanied by a substantial reduction in permeability. An optimum Terrazyme dosage of 2.0% was identified, which provided the maximum enhancement in strength and durability while significantly reducing the permeability of the investigated silty sand. These improvements are attributed to enhanced particle bonding, matrix densification, and physicochemical interactions promoted by the bioenzymatic treatment. The findings indicate that Terrazyme has the potential to serve as a sustainable and environmentally friendly alternative to conventional chemical stabilizers for the stabilization of silty sand and subgrade improvement. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the potential of bioenzymatic stabilization as a viable approach for developing resilient and sustainable geotechnical infrastructure.

title: Development and Evaluation of a Lapatinib-Loaded Lipomer Formulation for Pulmonary Drug Delivery
author: Mujawar, Nigar Kadar
abstract: Background Lung cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Lapatinib has shown therapeutic potential; however, its clinical application is limited by poor aqueous solubility and pharmacokinetic challenges. Therefore, the present study aimed to develop and evaluate a lapatinib-loaded lipomer formulation for pulmonary drug delivery. Purpose The present study aimed to formulate and evaluate a Lapatinib (LAP)-loaded lipomer system for improved delivery and enhanced therapeutic management of lung cancer. The research focused on developing a stable nanocarrier capable of increasing drug bioavailability, prolonging systemic circulation, and achieving sustained drug release with enhanced pulmonary accumulation. Methods LAP-loaded lipomers were prepared using the emulsification–solvent evaporation technique. Soya lecithin was used as the lipid component, stearylamine as the charge-inducing agent, and poly lactic acid (PLA) as the polymer matrix. The prepared formulation was lyophilized to obtain a stable freeze-dried lipomer. The formulation was characterized for particle size, polydispersity index (PDI), zeta potential, entrapment efficiency, drug content, and drug loading. Compatibility and structural studies were performed using FTIR, DSC, and XRD, while morphology was examined using SEM and TEM. Results The optimized lipomer showed a particle size of 125.4 nm with a PDI of 0.394 and a zeta potential of − 25.5 mV. Entrapment efficiency was 84.10%, drug content was 96.8 ± 2.1%, and drug loading was 18.5 ± 1.7%. Compatibility studies confirmed drug–excipient stability. The formulation exhibited sustained drug release (87.50% at 24 h) and improved cytotoxic activity against A549 lung cancer cells (IC₅₀ = 5.80 µg/mL) compared to pure LAP (9.40 µg/mL). Pharmacokinetic and biodistribution studies demonstrated prolonged circulation and higher lung accumulation. Conclusion The developed freeze-dried LAP-loaded lipomer demonstrated improved bioavailability, sustained drug release, enhanced lung accumulation, and good stability, indicating its potential as an effective nanocarrier system for lung cancer therapy.

title: Noncircadian BMAL1–YAP activity amplifies persistent inflammation in aged epidermis
author: Bonjoch, Júlia
abstract: Chronic inflammation is a hallmark of aging, yet the underlying molecular mechanisms are incompletely understood. Here the authors show that, in the skin, BMAL1 and YAP cooperate at enhancers to maintain epidermal homeostasis. During aging, this cooperation is increased at inflammatory enhancers, driven by age-associated changes in the microenvironment, promoting epidermal inflammation. Aging is characterized by persistent low-grade inflammation linked to impaired tissue homeostasis, yet the underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. The mammalian skin is a clinically relevant site of aging-driven inflammation associated with compromised barrier function, inefficient wound healing, elevated oxidative stress and DNA damage accumulation. Here we show that, in the murine epidermis, aging engages a previously uncharacterized BMAL1–YAP functional cooperation with enhanced binding at inflammation-related enhancers, amplifying target gene transcription. Independent of its circadian clock role, BMAL1 partners with the mechanosensitive cofactor YAP at enhancer regions to regulate epidermal identity genes. However, in aged skin, this cooperative binding undergoes a functional shift, enhancing the expression of inflammation-related genes, partially coregulated by NF-κB. In addition, aged pro-inflammatory IL-17 signaling activates YAP in a Hippo-independent manner. These findings unveil a transcriptional mechanism underlying epidermal aging, linking chromatin dynamics to inflammatory programs through rewiring of BMAL1–YAP-occupied enhancers, highlighting potential strategies to counteract chronic inflammation and restore tissue homeostasis during aging.

title: Applications of synthetic biology in biomedicine
author: Li, Chen-Xuan
abstract: Based on the principles of engineering reconstruction and programmable design, synthetic biology is driving a paradigm shift in biomedical diagnosis and therapy from conventional models toward intelligent and precision medicine. By constructing artificial genetic circuits, functional cells, and biomaterial systems both in vitro and in vivo, synthetic biology markedly enhances diagnostic sensitivity, therapeutic targeting, and clinical benefit. In recent years, with the maturation of key technologies such as DNA synthesis and assembly, computational modeling, gene editing, RNA regulation, and protein engineering, synthetic biology has spawned numerous applications with potential for clinical translation in fields such as early screening for pathogens and tumors, programmable cellular immunotherapies, intelligent life-based therapies, and the manufacture of medical biomaterials. Nevertheless, current synthetic biology systems still face critical bottlenecks such as insufficient targeting and editing precision in vivo, poor functional stability of gene circuits, pronounced immunogenicity risks, high manufacturing costs, and lagging ethical and regulatory frameworks. This review systematically summarizes progress in foundational tools and key supporting technologies of synthetic biology, highlights innovative strategies and clinical value in biosensors, cell therapy, living therapeutics, and smart biomaterials, and provides an in‑depth comparison of different chassis cells, delivery vectors, and regulatory circuits in terms of disease suitability, safety, and translational efficiency. The artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled component design, closed-loop intelligent regulation, off‑the‑shelf universal cells, and multimodal theranostic platforms are also discussed. This review offers a systematic framework from technical principles to clinical translation and provides theoretical support and technical guidance for developing next-generation synthetic biology-based diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.

title: Enhancing the tensile strength of nitrile rubber gloves with tribologically modified graphene via process parameter optimization using response surface methodology
author: Leong, Yien Leng
abstract: Nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR) is among the most widely used synthetic elastomers in protective glove manufacturing. However, scalable and cost-effective methods for producing graphene-reinforced NBR gloves with optimized tensile strength remain insufficiently explored. In the present study, graphene nanoplatelets (GNP) were tribologically modified with sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate (SDBS) via a microwave-assisted planetary ball-milling process and incorporated into NBR latex for glove fabrication. The tensile strength of the glove is optimized by Response Surface Methodology (RSM) and the GNP-NBR interfacial interaction is elucidated by density functional theory (DFT). The parameters of ball milling, microwave and latex compounding are optimized to maximize the tensile strength of the NBR glove. The maximum tensile strength achieved experimentally is 37.80 MPa, which shows only slightly lower tensile strength (39.03 MPa) than RSM-predicted value, implying the low prediction error (3.15%) of the RSM model. The optimized GNP/NBR glove shows an improvement of 23.93% compared to the bare NBR glove (30.5 MPa). Besides, the tensile strength of 37.80 MPa in optimized GNP/NBR glove is also higher than all previously reported values for graphene-reinforced nanocomposites by a minimum of 8%. The DFT simulation show that NBR-GNP is more thermodynamically favorable to interact in the dipole–π configuration due to the most negative adsorption energy (− 23.8616 kJ/mol). Electrostatic potential (ESP) mapping further confirmed high electron density at the GNP–NBR interface, corroborating the strong interfacial adhesion responsible for the observed tensile enhancement. This work provides a time and cost saving approach to systematically optimize multiple variables in GNP-NBR glove production, which is beneficial for scalable production in glove making industry.

title: Valorization of Pinus brutia bark and resin into eco-friendly biopolymer hydrogels for wound healing applications
author: Taş Küçükaydın, Meltem
abstract: The sustainable conversion of forestry by-products into bioactive biopolymer materials is a promising strategy for biodegradable wound dressing systems. This study valorized Pinus brutia bark extract (PBBE) and resin extract (PBRE) by incorporating them into chitosan-, chitosan/gelatin-, poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA)/chitosan-, and PVA/starch-based hydrogel films. The extracts were characterized by high-performance liquid chromatography with diode-array detection (HPLC-DAD) and gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS), and the films were evaluated for physicochemical properties, release behavior, biological activities, cytotoxicity, and scratch wound closure. PBBE showed a taxifolin-rich phenolic profile, with taxifolin as the major compound (180.5 mg/g), strong 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radical scavenging activity (IC_50: 7.33 µg/mL), and tyrosinase inhibition comparable to kojic acid. PBRE was dominated by diterpenic acids (87.43%) and exhibited notable antifungal activity against Candida albicans , with a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of 0.078 mg/mL. Among the hydrogel systems, chitosan-based films showed the highest swelling and degradation, with chitosan-PBBE reaching the highest swelling ratio (381.0%). Extract-loaded hydrogels also displayed pH-dependent release and improved functional performance depending on polymer composition and extract type. In the scratch assay, both extracts enhanced wound closure compared with untreated controls, with PBBE reaching 70.00% closure at 24 h and both extracts reaching complete closure at 72 h. The extracts showed no apparent cytotoxicity toward HEK-293T cells. Overall, these findings suggest that P. brutia bark and resin can serve as sustainable bioactive ingredients for biodegradable hydrogel films intended for wound dressing applications, although further validation using skin-relevant cell models and in vivo studies is required.

title: Konjac glucomannan biopolymer as a multifunctional binder to build a solid permeable interface on Na3V2(PO4)3/C cathodes for high-performance sodium ion batteries
author: Yuyao Zhang
abstract: The cathode materials for sodium ion batteries (SIBs) are intrinsically unstable due to their oxidation by electrolyte solution at high voltage; thus, developing novel solid permeable interfaces as passivation layers is critical to avoid these side oxidation reactions and increase the cycling durability of SIBs. Nevertheless, the abuse of passivation layers can hinder the Na+ transfer and further impact the rate capability. Herein, we demonstrated an effective approach that utilized konjac glucomannan (KGM) biopolymer as a multifunctional binder to build stable solid permeable interface films to achieve high-performance for Na3V2(PO4)3/C (NVP) cathodes. Compared with polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF), the strong adhesion and solid permeable interface films of KGM protect the integrity of the electrodes. The unique conductive network and rich polar functional groups enable KGM to enhance the transfer of electrons and Na+ ions at the interfaces. Thanks to the multiple functions of KGM offering adhesion strength, a conductive network and a solid permeable interface, the NVP cathode exhibited a reversible capacity of 108.0 mA h g−1 at 0.5C (1C = 117 mA g−1). At a high rate of 50C, NVP profited from KGM to show a good capacity of 63.1 mA h g−1 and a high durability of 10 000 cycles with a small fading rate of 0.00259% per cycle. Hard carbon‖NVP full batteries, using KGM as the cathode binder, possessed a high specific energy of 137.7 W h kg−1, indicating the potential applications of KGM as an environmentally friendly binder for achieving high-rate capacity and long-term cycling durability of SIBs.

title: A Novel UV Barrier Poly(lactic acid)/Poly(butylene succinate) Composite Biodegradable Film Enhanced by Cellulose Extracted from Coconut Shell
author: Xiaoyan He
abstract: Cellulose was extracted from coconut shell powder (CSP) as a renewable biomass resource and utilized as a reinforcing material in poly(lactic acid)/poly(butylene succinate) (PLA/PBS) solvent casting films. The extraction process involved delignification and mercerization of CSP. Microscopic investigation of the extracted microfibers demonstrated a reduction in diameter and a rougher surface characteristic compared to the raw CSP. The cellulose prepared in this study exhibited improved thermal stability and higher crystallinity (54.3%) compared to CSP. The morphology of the cycrofractured surface, thermal analysis, mechanical property, and UV transmittance of films were measured and compared. Agglomeration of 3 wt.% of cellulose was observed in PLA/PBS films. The presence of cellulose higher than 1 wt.% in the PLA/PBS decreased the onset decomposition temperature and maximum decomposition temperature of films. However, the films loading 3 wt.% of cellulose had a higher char formation (5.47%) compared to neat PLA/PBS films. The presence of cellulose promoted the formation of non-uniform crystals, while cellulose had a slightly negative impact on crystallinity due to the disruption of polymer chains at lower cellulose content (0.3, 0.5 wt.%). The mechanical strength of PLA/PBS films decreased as the cellulose content increased. Moreover, PLA/PBS film with 3 wt.% of cellulose appeared to show a 3% and 7.5% decrease in transmittance in UVC (275 nm) and UVA (335 nm) regions compared to neat PLA/PBS films while maintaining a certain transparency.

title: Characterization of Thin Film PLA/PBAT Reinforced with Microcrystalline Cellulose Derived from Gigantochloa albociliata
author: M. R. S. Fatimah
abstract: Microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) from bamboo is a natural biodegradable polymer that can be applied as barrier materials in the form of films. Bamboo contributes to 90% of the total mass of the dry weight comprised of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. In this study, Gigantochloaalbociliata (Buluh Madu) was chosen due to the fast-growing species, cheaper and abundance in Malaysia. This bamboo was undergone Kraft pulping process to get the pure cellulose and then continued with the acid hydrolysis process to produce microcrystalline cellulose (MCC). In this study, thin-film PLA/PBAT reinforced with microcrystalline cellulose derived from Gigantochloaalbociliata were produced. PLA is high in strength and ductility, but it is brittle while PBAT is elastic and strong. Therefore, PBAT is a great candidate for PLA hardness. The thin film was characterized with XRD, DSC and TGA to compare the thin film from microcrystalline cellulose derived from bamboo (B-MCC) with the commercial microcrystalline cellulose (C-MCC). The C-MCC was used as reference material. From the results, B-MCC has the same crystallinity index as C-MCC with a value of 51.3%. It can be concluded that B-MCC is can be one of the alternatives for the microcrystalline cellulose due to the abundance of bamboo as fast-growing species. Furthermore, it exists naturally, has low cost, is biodegradable, is a low-density compound, and fits best in the field of renewability.

title: Polylactic Acid-Based Film Modified with Nano-Ag-Graphene-TiO2: New Film versus Recycled Film
author: A. Peter
abstract: The increase in the polymer-based materials needs has induced along the waste accumulation, thus argued higher interest in recycling. The study aims to assess the structural, morphological, mechanical resistance, physical–chemical and biochemical characteristics, as well as the preservative role during the curd cheese storage of a recycled polylactic acid (PLA)-based film modified with Ag-graphene-TiO2 nanostructured composite, obtained by recovering the composite from the used film, followed by its incorporation in new PLA. The breaking load of the recycled film was 24% lower than that of the new film and 10% higher than of the neat PLA. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) showed changes of the recycled PLA’s surface tension and crystallization degree in a greater extent than in the newly prepared film, revealing better incorporation of the recovered composite into the PLA matrix. Fourier transformed infrared spectroscopy showed the formation of C–O–Ti bridges between composite and PLA both in new and recycled film. Oxygen transmission rate (OTR) of the new and recycled film decreased by 33% and 45%, respectively, in comparison with reference PLA. The curd cheese was successfully stored in the recycled packaging; the organoleptic characteristics of cheese wrapped in recycled film were superior in comparison with the new film. The variation of fat and protein contents and mass loss was the lowest when the recycled film was used as packaging material. The study successfully showed the possibility to recover and recycle the used PLA-based films modified with inorganic nanocomposites.

title: Effects of talc, kaolin and calcium carbonate as fillers in biopolymer packaging materials
author: Karoliina Helanto
abstract: Abstract We compared the performance of bio-based and biodegradable polymers for packaging applications. Cost-effective inorganic fillers (talc, kaolin and calcium carbonate) were first melt-compounded with polylactic acid (PLA), poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) and poly(hydroxy butyrate-co-valerate) (PHBV). Following this, injection- and compression-molded specimens were produced to test the effect of filler loading (0–30 wt%) in relation to the morphological, thermal, mechanical and barrier properties of the composites. All the fillers were homogeneously dispersed in the polymer matrices and suitable polymer–filler adhesion was observed for talc and kaolin. The elastic modulus increased at the expense of a reduced tensile and elongation. The most significant improvements in water vapor and oxygen barrier properties were achieved with talc in PLA, PBAT and PHBV films. Overall, the results point to the promise of the introduced compositions for food packaging materials.
